title: Space Movie Reveals Shocking Secrets of the Crab Pulsar
caption: The Crab pulsar, imaged by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Crab Pulsar · constellation Taurus · about 6000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA/CXC/ASU/J. Hester et al., HST/ASU/J. Hester et al.

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: This image comes from an unusual project, a space movie made by two of NASA's Great Observatories. Over several months, the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Hubble Space Telescope observed the Crab pulsar again and again, and the sequence of images was assembled to show change over time.

A pulsar is a kind of neutron star, the collapsed core left behind after a massive star explodes. The Crab pulsar spins rapidly, and it is extremely compact, with the collapsed remnant only about the size of Manhattan.

The pulsar hurls matter and antimatter outward at close to the speed of light. By watching the region repeatedly, astronomers could follow how this outflow behaves rather than seeing a single frozen moment, which is why the project was billed as an action movie. This still is one frame from that sequence.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.15 x 2.15 arcminutes) and distance (6000 light years), the frame spans roughly 3.8 × 3.8 light-years. Its light set out about 6,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The observations combine X-ray data from Chandra with Hubble images. The source does not list filters or publish a colour mapping.
understand.eye: X-rays are invisible to the eye, and the changes shown unfolded over months, far too slowly to watch directly.
